subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 12! You already know that a fraction is a way of showing part of a whole. In this unit you will become much more confident with fractions and learn four powerful new skills. You will discover equivalent fractions (different-looking fractions that are really worth the same), you will compare fractions to say which is bigger, you will find a fraction of an amount (like 1/4 of 20 mangoes), and you will add and subtract fractions that share the same bottom number.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 3 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Explain what equivalent fractions are and find them by multiplying or dividing.
Show equivalent fractions with pictures such as fraction strips and bars.
Compare two fractions and use the symbols >, < and =.
Compare fractions with the same denominator and with the same numerator.
Use benchmark fractions like 0, 1/2 and 1 to judge size.
Find a fraction of an amount by dividing then multiplying.
Add and subtract fractions that have the same denominator.
Simplify a fraction to its lowest terms after adding or subtracting.
Understand and write simple mixed numbers (for example 1¼ or 2½), and place fractions and mixed numbers in order on a number line.

concepts.title: Equivalent Fractions
concepts.explanation:
Equivalent fractions are different fractions that show the same amount of a whole. They may look different on the page, but they are worth exactly the same. This is one of the most useful ideas in all of fractions.

Picture a warm anjero, the flat bread many families eat. If Farah cuts it into 2 equal pieces and takes 1, she has eaten 1/2 of the anjero. Now picture the same anjero cut into 4 equal pieces. If she takes 2 of those pieces, she has eaten 2/4. Look at her plate both times – it is the very same amount of bread! So 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent fractions. They are two different names for one amount.

We can keep going. Cut the anjero into 6 equal pieces and take 3, and you have 3/6 – still one half. Cut it into 8 and take 4, and you have 4/8 – still one half. So 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8. All of these are equivalent, because in every case the shaded part is exactly half of the whole.

To find an equivalent fraction, multiply (or divide) the numerator and the denominator by the same number. This is the golden rule. Whatever you do to the top, you must do to the bottom.

Let us find some fractions equal to 1/3:

Multiply top and bottom by 2: 1/3 = (1×2)/(3×2) = 2/6

Multiply top and bottom by 3: 1/3 = (1×3)/(3×3) = 3/9

Multiply top and bottom by 4: 1/3 = (1×4)/(3×4) = 4/12

So 1/3 = 2/6 = 3/9 = 4/12. Every one of these is worth exactly one third. Why does this work? Because multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number is like cutting each piece of your anjero into smaller equal pieces. You now have more pieces (bigger denominator) but each is smaller, and you take more of them (bigger numerator), so the total amount on your plate does not change at all.

Let us try one more together so it feels natural. Start with 3/4 and find three fractions equal to it. Multiply top and bottom by 2 to get 6/8. Multiply by 3 to get 9/12. Multiply by 4 to get 12/16. So 3/4 = 6/8 = 9/12 = 12/16. If you draw a bar split into 4 with 3 shaded, then split the same bar into 8 with 6 shaded, the shaded strip is exactly the same length – proof that the two fractions are worth the same. Being able to make a whole family of equivalent fractions from one starting fraction is a skill you will use again and again when you compare, add and subtract.

Equivalent fractions also help in real life. Suppose a recipe for anjero asks for 1/2 cup of milk, but Aisha only has a 1/4 cup to measure with. Because 1/2 = 2/4, she knows she must fill the 1/4 cup twice. If another recipe asks for 3/4 cup of milk and she only has a 1/8 cup, she uses 3/4 = 6/8 to know she needs to fill the 1/8 cup six times. Equivalent fractions turn an awkward measuring job into a simple count.

Seeing equivalence with fraction strips
concepts.example: Imagine four paper strips of the same length, one above the other. The first is left whole (that is 1). The second is folded into 2 equal parts. The third is folded into 4 equal parts. The fourth is folded into 8 equal parts. If you shade 1 part of the halves strip, then lay it against the quarters strip, you see that it lines up exactly with 2 of the quarters, and with 4 of the eighths. Your eyes can see that 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. Fraction strips turn a rule into a picture you can trust.

concepts.title: Simplifying Fractions
concepts.explanation:
Simplifying a fraction means writing it in its lowest terms – using the smallest numbers possible while keeping the same value. To simplify, you divide the numerator and denominator by the same number.

Take 4/8. Both 4 and 8 can be divided by 4: 4÷4 = 1 and 8÷4 = 2, so 4/8 = 1/2. The fraction 1/2 is the simplest name for that amount. Take 6/9: both 6 and 9 can be divided by 3, giving 2/3, so 6/9 = 2/3.
concepts.example: A fraction is in its lowest terms when the numerator and denominator share no common factor except 1. For example, 3/5 is already simplest, because 3 and 5 have nothing in common except 1. Simplifying is very handy after adding or subtracting fractions, because it gives the neatest possible answer. When you finish a fraction calculation, always ask yourself: can this answer be simplified?

concepts.title: Comparing Fractions
concepts.explanation:
To compare two fractions is to decide which one is bigger, which is smaller, or whether they are equal. There are several neat ways to do this, and you choose the easiest one for the fractions in front of you.

Same denominator: look at the numerators

When two fractions have the same denominator (same bottom number), comparing is easy: the fraction with the bigger numerator is bigger. This makes sense – if the pieces are all the same size, then whoever has more pieces has more.

Compare 2/5 and 3/5. Both have denominator 5, so the pieces are the same size. Since 3 is more than 2, 3/5 > 2/5. If Yusuf eats 3 slices of a bariis dish cut into fifths and Omar eats 2 slices, Yusuf ate more.

Same numerator: look at the denominators

When two fractions have the same numerator (same top number), the fraction with the smaller denominator is bigger. This one surprises many learners, so think it through carefully.

Compare 2/3 and 2/5. Both have numerator 2. Imagine cutting the same mango into 3 equal pieces versus 5 equal pieces. When you cut into only 3 pieces, each piece is bigger than when you cut into 5 pieces. So 1/3 of a mango is bigger than 1/5 of a mango, which means 2/3 > 2/5. The fewer the pieces you cut, the bigger each piece is.

Different top and bottom: use equivalent fractions

When the numerators and denominators are different, the safest way is to change both fractions into equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then compare the numerators.

Find a common denominator. 12 works, because it is in both the 3 times table and the 4 times table.

Change 2/3: 2/3 = (2×4)/(3×4) = 8/12.

Change 3/4: 3/4 = (3×3)/(4×3) = 9/12.

Now compare 8/12 and 9/12. Since 9 is more than 8, 9/12 > 8/12.

Another clever way is to compare each fraction to a benchmark you know well, especially 1/2. Ask: is this fraction more than a half, or less than a half? A fraction is more than 1/2 when its numerator is more than half of its denominator.

Compare 3/8 and 4/7. Half of 8 is 4, and 3 is less than 4, so 3/8 is less than 1/2. Half of 7 is 3.5, and 4 is more than 3.5, so 4/7 is more than 1/2. Since 4/7 is above the halfway mark and 3/8 is below it, 4/7 > 3/8 – and we did not need a common denominator at all.

You can also picture fractions on a number line from 0 to 1. Mark the halfway point at 1/2. A fraction close to the right-hand end (near 1) is large; a fraction close to the left-hand end (near 0) is small. Placing fractions on a line like this helps you *see* which is bigger, just as you would see which of two markers on a road is further along. To place 3/4 on the line, split the road from 0 to 1 into four equal steps and mark the third step; to place 1/4, mark the first step. Straight away you can see that 3/4 sits further to the right, so 3/4 > 1/4.
concepts.example: When two fractions have the same denominator (same bottom number), comparing is easy: the fraction with the bigger numerator is bigger. This makes sense – if the pieces are all the same size, then whoever has more… Fractions also have a home on the number line, and placing them there helps you compare and order them at a glance. Draw a line from 0 to 1 and divide it into equal parts to match the denominator: for quarters, mark 0, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 1 evenly spaced along the line, with the smallest fraction closest to 0 and the largest closest to 1. Sometimes an amount is worth more than one whole – for example, if you eat 5 quarter-slices of bread, you have eaten more than 1 whole loaf. We write amounts like this as mixed numbers, which combine a whole number and a fraction together, such as 1¼ (one and a quarter) or 2½ (two and a half). To change an improper fraction like 5/4 into a mixed number, divide the numerator by the denominator: 5 ÷ 4 = 1 remainder 1, so 5/4 = 1¼. On the number line, mixed numbers simply continue past 1: 1¼ sits a quarter of the way between 1 and 2, and 2½ sits exactly halfway between 2 and 3.

concepts.title: Finding a Fraction of an Amount
concepts.explanation:
Finding a fraction of an amount means working out a part of a whole number of things. For example, finding 1/4 of 20 means splitting 20 into 4 equal groups and taking 1 group. This skill is used every day when you share things fairly.

Divide the amount by the denominator (the bottom number).

Multiply your answer by the numerator (the top number).

Let us find 3/5 of 20. First divide 20 by 5: 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Then multiply by 3: 4 × 3 = 12. So 3/5 of 20 is 12. The first step shares the whole into equal groups; the second step takes as many groups as the numerator asks for.

Notice why the order works. Dividing by the denominator tells you how big one of the equal parts is. Multiplying by the numerator then counts how many of those parts you want. If you only want 1 part (numerator 1), the second step is simply times 1, which changes nothing – so 1/5 of 20 is just 20 ÷ 5 = 4.

Find 1/4 of 28. Divide 28 ÷ 4 = 7, then multiply by 1: 7 × 1 = 7. So 1/4 of 28 is 7.

Find 2/3 of 18. Divide 18 ÷ 3 = 6, then multiply by 2: 6 × 2 = 12. So 2/3 of 18 is 12.

Find 3/4 of 32. Divide 32 ÷ 4 = 8, then multiply by 3: 8 × 3 = 24. So 3/4 of 32 is 24.

Picture 2/5 of 15 mangoes. First share the 15 mangoes into 5 equal groups, so each group has 3 mangoes. Then take 2 of those groups: 3 + 3 = 6. So 2/5 of 15 is 6 mangoes. Drawing the groups makes the method easy to trust.
concepts.example: This idea appears everywhere once you look. If a gift for a teacher at Nuur Academy costs 30 shillings and three friends agree that each will pay 1/3 of the cost, then each pays 30 ÷ 3 = 10 shillings. If Zahra has collected 20 litres of water and uses 3/4 of it for washing, she uses (20 ÷ 4) × 3 = 5 × 3 = 15 litres. Whenever you hear ‘a fraction of something’, that little word ‘of’ is a signal to divide by the denominator and multiply by the numerator.

concepts.title: Adding Fractions with the Same Denominator
concepts.explanation:
When two fractions have the same denominator, adding them is simple: add the numerators and keep the denominator the same. The denominator does not change because the pieces are all the same size – you are just counting how many pieces you have in total.

To add 1/5 + 2/5: add the numerators, 1 + 2 = 3, and keep the denominator 5. So 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5. Think of a bariis dish cut into 5 equal slices. If you take 1 slice and then 2 more, you have 3 slices out of 5 – that is 3/5.

Picture 1/4 + 2/4. Shade 1 quarter of a bar, then shade 2 more quarters. Altogether 3 quarters are shaded, so 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. The bar was always in quarters, so the bottom number stayed 4 throughout.

Sometimes the answer can be simplified. For example, 2/8 + 2/8 = 4/8, and 4/8 simplifies to 1/2. Other times it cannot: 2/6 + 3/6 = 5/6, and 5/6 is already in its lowest terms because 5 and 6 share no common factor except 1. Always check your answer at the end to see whether it simplifies.

One lovely thing happens when the numerators add up to the denominator. Take 2/3 + 1/3 = 3/3. But 3/3 means all three parts of a whole – that is one whole, or 1. So if Hassan pours 2/3 of a cup of white flour and 1/3 of a cup of wheat flour into the bowl, he has exactly 1 whole cup of flour.
concepts.example: Let us do two more so the method becomes automatic. To work out 5/12 + 3/12, add the numerators 5 + 3 = 8 and keep the denominator 12, giving 8/12. Can it be simplified? Yes – both 8 and 12 divide by 4, so 8/12 = 2/3. To work out 1/4 + 1/4, add the numerators 1 + 1 = 2 and keep the denominator 4, giving 2/4, which simplifies to 1/2. Each time the pattern is the same: add the tops, keep the bottom, then simplify if you can. Once you have done a handful of these, your hand will do it almost without thinking.

concepts.title: Subtracting Fractions with the Same Denominator
concepts.explanation:
Subtracting fractions with the same denominator works the same friendly way: subtract the numerators and keep the denominator the same.

To work out 4/6 - 1/6: subtract the numerators, 4 - 1 = 3, and keep the denominator 6. So 4/6 - 1/6 = 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2. If a jug holds 6 equal cups of water and is filled to 4/6, and you pour out 1/6, then 3/6 (a half) is still in the jug.

Picture 3/8 - 1/8. Start with 3 of 8 equal parts shaded, then rub out 1 part. You are left with 2 shaded parts, so 3/8 - 1/8 = 2/8, which simplifies to 1/4. Again the denominator stays 8, because the whole is always in eighths; only the number of parts changes.

You have now met six big ideas: equivalent fractions, simplifying, comparing fractions, finding a fraction of an amount, adding fractions, and subtracting fractions. These ideas are not separate islands – they help one another. When you compare 2/3 and 3/4, you use equivalent fractions to give them a common denominator. When you finish adding two fractions, you use simplifying to write the tidiest answer. When you find 2/5 of 15 mangoes, you are really sharing a whole into equal parts, which is exactly what a denominator means.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these ideas into your memory is to use them with real things around your home. Share dates equally at iftar and name the fraction each person gets. Fold a piece of paper to show that 1/2 and 2/4 are the same. Pour water into a cup and describe how full it is as a fraction. Every time you do this, your fraction sense grows stronger, and the harder maths in later years will feel much easier. Now let us practise together with some worked examples.

methods.title: How to find a fraction of an amount
steps: Divide the amount by the denominator (bottom number).
Multiply your answer by the numerator (top number).
Check your answer by multiplying it back up: your answer × denominator should equal the amount you started with.

methods.title: How to compare two fractions
steps: If the denominators match, compare the numerators.
If the numerators match, the smaller denominator wins.
Otherwise, change both to the same denominator and compare.

methods.title: How to simplify a fraction
steps: Find a number that divides both the top and the bottom.
Divide both by that number.
Repeat until the only common factor left is 1.

methods.title: Compare two fractions
steps: Use a common denominator of 15.

methods.title: Find a fraction of an amount
methods.example: In a class of 30 pupils at Nuur Academy, 2/5 walk to school. How many walk?
steps: Divide 30 ÷ 5 = 6, then multiply by 2: 6 × 2 = 12.
So 12 pupils walk to school.
Check by working backwards: 12 ÷ 2 × 5 should bring you back to 30.

methods.title: Add fractions
methods.example: Work out 3/8 + 2/8 and simplify if you can.
steps: Add the numerators: 3 + 2 = 5.
Keep the denominator 8.
Since 5 and 8 share no common factor, it is already in lowest terms.

workedExamples.title: Find three equivalent fractions
workedExamples.solution: Multiply top and bottom by the same number each time. ×2 gives 4/6; ×3 gives 6/9; ×4 gives 8/12. So 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9 = 8/12. Each shows the same amount.

workedExamples.title: Fill in the missing number
workedExamples.solution: The denominator went from 5 to 10, which is ×2. So multiply the top by 2 as well: 3 × 2 = 6. The missing number is 6, so 3/5 = 6/10.

workedExamples.title: Simplify a fraction
workedExamples.solution: Both 10 and 15 divide by 5. 10 ÷ 5 = 2 and 15 ÷ 5 = 3. So 10/15 = 2/3, which cannot be simplified further.

workedExamples.title: Find a fraction of an amount
workedExamples.prompt: In a class of 30 pupils at Nuur Academy, 2/5 walk to school. How many walk?
workedExamples.solution: Divide 30 ÷ 5 = 6, then multiply by 2: 6 × 2 = 12. So 12 pupils walk to school.

workedExamples.title: Add fractions
workedExamples.prompt: Work out 3/8 + 2/8 and simplify if you can.
workedExamples.solution: Add the numerators: 3 + 2 = 5. Keep the denominator 8. So 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8. Since 5 and 8 share no common factor, it is already in lowest terms.

workedExamples.title: Subtract fractions
workedExamples.prompt: A jug is 5/6 full. Halima pours out 2/6 of the jug. What fraction is still filled?
workedExamples.solution: Subtract the numerators: 5 — 2 = 3. Keep the denominator 6. So 5/6 — 2/6 = 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2. Half the jug is still filled.

workedExamples.title: Add to make a whole
workedExamples.prompt: Amina eats 2/8 of a mango pie and Sahra eats 3/8. What fraction did they eat together?
workedExamples.solution: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8. So together they ate 5/8 of the pie, and 3/8 was left over.

workedExamples.title: Add and simplify where possible
workedExamples.prompt: Add and simplify where possible: a) 2/8 + 2/8 b) 2/6 + 3/6 c) 1/4 + 1/4.

workedExamples.title: Subtract and simplify where possible
workedExamples.prompt: Subtract and simplify where possible: a) 4/6 — 1/6 b) 6/8 — 2/8.

workedExamples.title: Fill in to make equivalent fractions
workedExamples.prompt: Fill in to make equivalent fractions: a) 3/5 = □/10 b) 2/3 = 8/□ c) □/4 = 3/12.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Which is greater, 2/3 or 3/4? Convert both to twelfths and explain.
workedExamples.solution: Convert to twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Since 9/12 > 8/12, 3/4 is greater than 2/3.

activities.title: Fraction Strips
activities.materials: strips of paper of equal length, a pencil, and a ruler.
steps: Take four strips of the same length. Keep the first whole and label it 1.
Fold the second into 2 equal parts; label each part 1/2.
Fold the third into 4 equal parts; label each 1/4. Fold the fourth into 8; label each 1/8.
Lay the strips under each other. Line up 1/2 against the quarters and eighths – what equivalent fractions can you see?
You should find that 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. Keep your strips to use all through this unit.

activities.title: Fold and Share the Anjero
activities.materials: a round piece of paper (a pretend anjero) and a pencil.
steps: Fold your paper anjero in half, then in half again, to make 4 equal parts.
Shade 2 of the 4 parts. What fraction is shaded? Is it the same as 1/2?
Now fold a fresh anjero into 8 equal parts and shade 4. Is this still one half?
Explain to a family member why 2/4 and 4/8 are both equal to 1/2.

activities.title: The Fraction Compare Card Game
activities.materials: paper cards, each with one fraction written on it (for example 1/2, 2/5, 3/4, 2/3, 3/8).
steps: Shuffle the cards and place them face down.
Each player turns over one card.
Compare the two fractions – whoever has the bigger fraction wins both cards.
If it is tricky, change both fractions to the same denominator to be sure. Play until the cards run out.
This game trains you to compare fractions quickly and fairly.

activities.title: Fraction of a Set (Counting Investigation)
activities.materials: 24 small objects such as stones, beans or bottle caps.
steps: Count out 24 objects.
Find 1/3 of them: share the objects into 3 equal groups and count one group.
Find 2/3 of them: count two of the groups.
Try again with different numbers, such as 1/4 of 20 or 3/5 of 15. Write down each answer.

activities.title: Fraction Addition Game (Family or Group)
activities.materials: cards with same-denominator fractions (for example many eighths and many sixths), paper and a pencil.
steps: Shuffle the cards and deal two to each player, making sure both share a denominator.
Each player adds or subtracts their two fractions and writes the answer.
Simplify the answer if you can – earn a bonus point for simplifying correctly.
The player with the most points after several rounds wins.

activities.title: Kitchen Fraction Hunt
activities.materials: a helpful adult and safe kitchen items (a measuring cup, a bowl of dates).
steps: Find something you can measure in fractions, such as a 1/4 cup or a 1/2 cup.
Use the 1/4 cup twice – how many quarters make one half? Show that 2/4 = 1/2.
Count a bowl of dates and find 1/2 and then 1/4 of them by sharing into groups.
Tell your family one place where fractions are used in cooking.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand equivalent fractions best? What was the trickiest part of comparing or adding fractions? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Equivalent Fractions Rule
rules.text: Multiply (or divide) the top and bottom by the SAME number. 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8. Adding the same number to top and bottom does NOT work.

rules.title: Comparing Rule
rules.text: Same denominator: the bigger numerator is the bigger fraction. Same numerator: the smaller denominator is the bigger fraction. Otherwise: change to the same denominator, then compare.

rules.title: Add and Subtract Rule
rules.text: Same denominator: add or subtract the numerators only. Keep the denominator the same. Simplify the answer if you can.

realProblems.prompt: At the Kismaayo market, Idris buys 20 mangoes and sells 3/4 of them by noon. How many did he sell, and how many are left?
realProblems.answer: 3/4 of 20 = 15 mangoes sold, so 20 − 15 = 5 mangoes are left.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the question is really about (Numerator, Denominator, Equivalent fractions), then work one step at a time and check the answer is sensible.
realProblems.errorFeedback: 3/4 of 20 = 15 mangoes sold, so 20 − 15 = 5 mangoes are left.

realProblems.prompt: During iftar, a family shares a plate of sambusa cut into 8 equal pieces. Aisha eats 2/8 and Ibrahim eats 3/8. What fraction did they eat together, and what fraction remains?
realProblems.answer: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8 eaten together, so 8/8 − 5/8 = 3/8 of the plate remains.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the question is really about (Numerator, Denominator, Equivalent fractions), then work one step at a time and check the answer is sensible.
realProblems.errorFeedback: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8 eaten together, so 8/8 − 5/8 = 3/8 of the plate remains.

realProblems.prompt: Noor walks from home to the masjid. She has covered 2/5 of the journey. What fraction of the journey is still ahead of her?
realProblems.answer: The whole journey is 5/5. She has covered 2/5, so 5/5 − 2/5 = 3/5 of the journey is still ahead.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the question is really about (Numerator, Denominator, Equivalent fractions), then work one step at a time and check the answer is sensible.
realProblems.errorFeedback: The whole journey is 5/5. She has covered 2/5, so 5/5 − 2/5 = 3/5 of the journey is still ahead.

realProblems.prompt: A recipe needs 3/4 cup of flour. Zahra wants to make half of the recipe. How much flour does she need? (Hint: find 1/2 of 3/4 by halving — think of 3/4 as 6/8.)
realProblems.answer: Half of 3/4 is 3/8 cup (3/4 = 6/8, and half of 6/8 = 3/8).
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the question is really about (Numerator, Denominator, Equivalent fractions), then work one step at a time and check the answer is sensible.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Half of 3/4 is 3/8 cup (3/4 = 6/8, and half of 6/8 = 3/8).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Which is greater, 2/3 or 3/4? Convert both to twelfths and explain.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Convert to twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Since 9/12 > 8/12, 3/4 is greater than 2/3.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Which fraction is closer to 1/2, 3/8 or 5/8? Explain how you know.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 1/2 = 4/8. 3/8 is 1/8 less than 4/8, and 5/8 is 1/8 more than 4/8 — so both fractions are exactly the same distance from 1/2, just on opposite sides.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Find a fraction that is greater than 1/3 but less than 1/2.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: One example is 2/5: since 1/3 ≈ 0.33 and 1/2 = 0.5, and 2/5 = 0.4 sits between them. (Other correct answers exist, such as 5/12 or 3/7.)

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A jug is 5/6 full. If 2/6 of the jug is poured out, what fraction is still filled? Simplify your answer.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2. Half the jug is still filled.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Halima says 1/4 is bigger than 1/3 because 4 is bigger than 3. Is she right? Explain.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: No, Halima is wrong. When the numerator is the same, a bigger denominator means smaller pieces (the whole is split into more parts), so 1/3 is actually bigger than 1/4, not smaller.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Subtracting Fractions with the Same Denominator.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Subtracting fractions with the same denominator works the same friendly way: subtract the numerators and keep the denominator the same. To work out 4/6 - 1/6: subtract the numerators, 4 - 1 = 3, and keep the denominator 6. So 4/6 - 1/6 = 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2. If a jug holds 6 equal cups of water and is filled to 4/6, and you pour out 1/6, then 3/6 (a half) is still in the jug.
